implementation_notes: Scala pools live in the JVM ecosystem, so the realisation is a library configuration: Slick's Database.forConfig builds a HikariCP pool straight from Typesafe Config (`connectionPool = "HikariCP"`, dataSourceClass without its own pooling) and Database.forDataSource(dataSource, Some(size)) plugs in a pool you already own - the size argument must match the DataSource's real limit or Slick queues against a cap it cannot see. On top of the pool sits the AsyncExecutor thread pool, which is the number to tune for concurrency; Slick points at HikariCP's pool-sizing guidance, and it recommends enabling prepared-statement caching in the pool because Slick itself does not cache statements. Cats Effect and ZIO add Resource/Pool wrappers, but the underlying borrowed-connection structure is the same JVM pool.
code_sketch:
val db = Database.forConfig("mydb")   // connectionPool = "HikariCP", and a thread pool
val io: Future[Seq[User]] = db.run(users.filter(_.id === 1).result)   // borrow + release
pitfalls: Two capacities compete - the connection pool and the AsyncExecutor thread pool; sizing only one starves the other, so follow the pool-sizing guidance rather than picking round numbers.
A blocking action inside db.run occupies a pool slot for its whole duration while threads queue behind it, so size the pool for the worst-case action and keep blocking work off the execution context.
The pool is a heavyweight object owning threads, sockets and prepared-statement caches: create one per application, and close it (db.close) on shutdown or every reload leaks it.
